PHSCS 587

Density of states

From the figure to the concept

Fig. 1 shows how one-, two- and three-dimensional bands supply different numbers of states

Confinement changes carrier population even before occupation is considered. The density of states g(E) counts allowed states per energy and per length, area or volume. For a parabolic dispersion with an isolated subband edge E0, g(E) scales as (E − E0)^(d/2 − 1) in dimension d. The figure uses separate normalizations to compare shapes: an ideal 1D edge has an integrable inverse-square-root singularity, a 2D subband adds a step, and a 3D band rises as a square root.

For an isotropic 3D parabolic band, g3D(E) = [gs gv/(4π²)](2md/ℏ²)^(3/2)√(E − EC) for E ≥ EC. gs counts spin states, gv counts equivalent valleys, md is the single-valley DOS mass in kg, and ℏ is Planck’s constant divided by 2π. With joule energies this gives states/(J·m³). A 2D subband beginning at Ej instead has g2D(E) = gs gv md/(2πℏ²) above Ej, in states/(J·m²). A valley factor must appear exactly once; an effective mass that already incorporates valleys uses a different convention.

Multiply DOS by Fermi occupation and integrate to obtain density: n = ∫ g3D(E)f(E)dE, or sheet density ns = Σj∫ g2D,j(E)f(E)dE. The latter is per area, so it cannot be substituted for a volume density without a spatial distribution or thickness model. To convert SI DOS per joule per m^d to DOS per eV per cm^d, multiply by q/100^d. Finite broadening or finite plotting resolution regularizes an ideal 1D edge.

Example

If two independent equivalent valleys have the same band edge and mass, their DOS contributions add. At fixed EF and T, doubling valley degeneracy doubles the carrier density contributed by those valleys.

Practice

1. Why does a second occupied 2D subband add another DOS step?

Count independent sets of in-plane states.

Each subband has its own constant in-plane DOS above its edge. Their contributions sum, so crossing a new edge adds its step.

2. What units distinguish a 2D carrier density from a 3D density?

Consider the unconfined dimensions.

A 2D density is carriers per area, such as cm⁻²; a 3D density is carriers per volume, such as cm⁻³.
